machines.finding: Researchers measure the vertical travel of the weight plates (not the handle) and treat plate mass x plate travel as the external work; leg extension stack travel measured with a tape to a per-subject mark at full extension, velocity = travel / concentric time.
Load-velocity studies of these two exercises also recorded vertical ascent of the weight plates (reported by Balsalobre-Fernandez 2019, citing Perez-Castilla 2019).

machines.notes: No peer-reviewed measurement found. Search results were blogs, equipment sellers, calculators and a patent, all excluded.

machines.finding: Geometric identity only: vertical rise = sled travel x sin(sled angle). Not a sourced measurement; sled travel and sled mass vary by machine and were not found in allowed sources.
machines.notes: Reis 2017 used a 45-deg leg press and gives loads (Table 1-2) but not sled mass or travel.

muscle_mass_scaling.finding: At the same relative load (12-24% 1RM, 15 reps/min), energy rate was highest for half squat and lowest for biceps curl; lower-body > upper-body at every intensity.
muscle_mass_scaling.notes: Per-minute rates at fixed cadence; not normalised to work. Loads in kg are in energy_sets so code can compute cost per kg-rep.

muscle_mass_scaling.finding: At 80% 1RM, anaerobic share of energy was above 50% for most exercises but below 50% for biceps curl and lat pulldown; authors link a larger aerobic share to smaller muscle mass.

Total external load lifted did not predict session energy across formats: BodyPump women lifted more (19,485 vs 15,616 kg incl. body-mass fractions) yet energy was similar (302 vs 289 kcal). Authors suggest smaller range of motion at ~1 rep/s in BodyPump.
muscle_mass_scaling.notes: Their 'workload' is load x reps (no displacement), which is exactly the gap a displacement term is meant to close.
